red_flags: Saddle anesthesia, urinary retention/incontinence, or bilateral leg weakness — cauda equina
Progressive focal neurological deficit (foot drop, worsening numbness)
Back pain with fever — spinal infection or TB until excluded
Known malignancy with new back pain
Significant trauma, or minimal trauma in an osteoporotic or steroid-treated patient
Pain waking the patient at night, unrelieved by rest
Age > 50 with new pain and weight loss
Sudden severe back/abdominal pain with hypotension, collapse, or a pulsatile abdominal mass — ruptured aortic aneurysm
exam: Observe gait and posture; look for deformity or a gibbus
Palpate spinous processes — focal bony tenderness vs paraspinal muscle spasm
Measure lumbar flexion and extension range
Straight-leg raise and crossed straight-leg raise
Lower-limb neurology: power (especially ankle/great-toe dorsiflexion), knee and ankle reflexes, dermatomal sensation
Perianal sensation and anal tone whenever cauda equina is suspected
Modified Schober test and chest expansion for spondyloarthritis
Percuss the renal angles for tenderness
Palpate the abdomen for a pulsatile expansile mass in patients > 60 or with sudden atraumatic pain
Examine hip rotation to exclude hip disease referring to the back

investigations.why: First-line when trauma, osteoporosis risk, or chronic features exist: shows vertebral collapse, lytic/sclerotic metastatic lesions, disc-space destruction of TB, or sacroiliitis of ankylosing spondylitis
Raised markers separate infection, spinal TB, and metastasis from mechanical pain and disc prolapse, where they stay normal
Anemia supports malignant infiltration; leukocytosis supports spinal infection
Raised ALP or disturbed calcium supports bony metastasis; part of the fragility-fracture workup
Prostate carcinoma is a common source of blastic spinal metastasis presenting as back pain
Hematuria supports ureteric stone when pain is colicky loin-to-groin; pyuria points to renal infection referring to the back
If renal colic is suspected: shows stone or hydronephrosis without irradiation
Second-line — urgent the same day for cauda equina signs; otherwise if radiculopathy persists > 6 weeks or infection, TB, or metastasis is suspected
